questions.q: List three non-English expressions used in the essay and identify their language of origin.
questions.a: "Mens sana in corpore sano" (Latin), "C'est la vie!" (French), "Nirvana" (Sanskrit). A wrong answer (e.g., listing "tremulations" or "cul-de-sac" as non-English) reveals the student cannot distinguish between coined English words, naturalized loanwords, and foreign phrases deliberately kept untranslated for rhetorical effect.

questions.q: In the phrase "the ugly imperialism of any absolute" (p. 170), what does "imperialism" mean in this context? Explain using the surrounding sentences.
questions.a: Here "imperialism" metaphorically means the tyrannical imposition of a single fixed idea ("absolute") over the fluid, multiplicitous reality of life. The context clues: "Once and for all and for ever, let us have done with the ugly imperialism of any absolute. There is no absolute good... All things flow and change." A wrong answer giving the historical/political definition ("policy of extending a country's power") shows failure to recognize metaphorical extension in philosophical argument.

questions.q: Using context clues from the paragraph beginning "Let us learn from the novel..." (p. 170), determine the meaning of "cul-de-sac" and explain why Lawrence chooses this metaphor.
questions.a: Steps: 1) Locate sentence: "A particular direction ends in a cul-de-sac." 2) Note preceding context: "I don't want to grow in any one direction any more." 3) Note following context: "We're in a cul-de-sac at present." 4) Infer meaning: a dead-end street, a situation with no exit. 5) Connect to argument: rigid consistency (always "good" or always "bad") stops growth/life. Lawrence uses the French term to emphasize the cultural/intellectual dead-end of fixed patterns. Wrong answer (e.g., "a curved road") reveals inability to use contrast clues ("I don't want to grow in one direction" vs. "cul-de-sac").

questions.q: Compare the meanings of "tremulations on the ether" when applied to (a) books/philosophy/science and (b) the novel. How does the same phrase carry opposite evaluations?
questions.a: For books/philosophy/science: "tremulations on the ether" = dead, disembodied vibrations that are "not alive at all" (p. 167), mere "radio messages" that cannot give life. For the novel: "the novel as a tremulation can make the whole man alive tremble" (p. 168) — it transmits life *to* life. The difference: philosophy's tremulations originate from a *part* (intellect/spirit) and remain partial; the novel's tremulation originates from *wholeness* and reaches wholeness. Wrong answer (e.g., "both mean vibrations") shows failure to track the essay's central part-vs-whole dialectic.

questions.q: Lawrence writes: "The whole is greater than the part. And therefore, I, who am man alive, am greater than my soul, or spirit, or body, or mind..." Evaluate whether "greater" here means "superior in value" or "more comprehensive in scope." Justify with context.
questions.a: "Greater" means more comprehensive in scope (mereological, not axiological). Context: "I absolutely flatly deny that I am a soul, or a body, or a mind... The whole is greater than the part." Lawrence rejects hierarchy (soul > body) in favor of inclusion: the living whole *contains* soul, body, mind but is not reducible to any. "Superior in value" would contradict his attack on philosophers who "decide that nothing but thoughts matter" (privileging one part). Wrong answer reveals confusion between hierarchical and part-whole reasoning.

questions.q: Write a 4-sentence paragraph continuing Lawrence's argument, using *tremulations*, *cul-de-sac*, *incongruous*, and *integrity* with their essay-specific meanings.
questions.a: Sample: "A philosophy that hardens into a fixed system sends dead tremulations into a cul-de-sac of abstraction. Life, by contrast, is an incongruous assembly of shifting parts that refuses any single pattern. True integrity is not consistency but the courage to remain whole amid contradiction. Only the novel, trembling with the full mess of living, can guide us there." Good answer uses each word in Lawrence's sense (tremulations=living communication, cul-de-sac=dead end of fixed pattern, incongruous=mismatched parts of living self, integrity=wholeness not rigidity). Poor answer uses dictionary definitions ignoring context.
